title: A visual-cortex prosthesis that restores useful, detailed sight

concept.text: The proposed innovation is an implanted system that translates external visual information, such as camera input, into stimulation of the visual cortex that a person can use as detailed, practical sight. Its goal is a stable visual representation that supports everyday activities, including navigation, recognizing faces and reading. This would require much more than eliciting isolated points of light, known as phosphenes, or recognizable simple shapes.

The system would combine a durable brain interface with a method for encoding visual information into spatial and temporal stimulation patterns. Translating camera input is a system-level formulation of the encoding challenge; the supplied evidence does not establish a camera-to-cortex pipeline that already delivers this level of sight. The intended capability remains hypothetical.

significance.text: If achieved, useful cortical vision could restore access to visual information for some people whose eyes or optic nerves cannot transmit it. Independent navigation, face recognition and ordinary reading would represent a major restorative advance because stimulation would convey information directly to brain circuits downstream of the failed transmission pathway. These benefits depend on effective visual encoding and safe, durable stimulation; they have not been demonstrated at the proposed level in the supplied record.

Mechanistic synthesis: this approach would depend on surviving visual circuits that can respond to stimulation and support useful perception. That is a reasoned boundary on the concept, rather than an established clinical eligibility rule in the supplied evidence. Extensive destruction of the necessary circuits would require additional restorative advances. Bypassing damaged upstream structures does not by itself repair those structures or recreate all the functions of natural vision.

Conditional downstream possibilities include greater independence in travel, communication, education and work. Their extent would depend on the information the prosthesis actually conveys, training requirements and performance outside controlled settings. Success on selected tasks would not establish natural visual acuity, a natural visual field or suitability for every cause of blindness.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central missing capability is a reliable mapping from visual information to stimulation, neural activity and useful perception. The July 2025 perspective identifies understanding the relationship between stimulation, neural activity and behavior as a critical hurdle. Evoking percepts establishes that cortical stimulation can produce visual experiences, but does not establish how to construct a stable, detailed scene from them. Spatial and temporal stimulation patterns must convey information that recipients can interpret consistently.

Resolution and visual-field coverage must improve together. Fine stimulation over a small cortical region does not automatically provide a broad usable field, while broader stimulation does not automatically preserve detail. Increasing stimulation intensity also encounters tissue-safety constraints: the perspective identifies tissue-damage risks from high currents. A successful interface must therefore achieve useful precision and coverage within safe stimulation limits.

Durability is a separate engineering and biological barrier. The perspective describes chronic variability in stimulation thresholds and adverse tissue responses, which can undermine a consistent relationship between device settings and perception. An interface must remain effective over time while limiting tissue injury, and its encoding must remain usable as the interface and its interaction with tissue change. These are documented barriers in the 2025 account; the supplied record does not establish their subsequent resolution or persistence through November 2026.

current_state.text: Kim and colleagues’ perspective, “Towards precise synthetic neural codes: high-dimensional stimulation with flexible electrodes,” published on 14 July 2025, describes human shape perception using dynamically steered surface stimulation of the visual cortex. It also reports shape perception in monkeys using patterned stimulation through 14 Utah electrode arrays implanted in primary visual cortex, V1. These reports provide a technical basis for patterned cortical visual stimulation, but do not demonstrate independent navigation, face recognition and ordinary reading through a detailed cortical visual scene.

The perspective identifies inadequate resolution, limited visual-field coverage and stimulation safety as major limitations. Its discussion also connects the broader prospects for neural stimulation to chronic interface stability and the difficulty of mapping stimulation to behavior. The evidence therefore supports a progression from evoked phosphenes toward shape perception, while leaving the proposed practical-sight capability unestablished.

These experimental descriptions come from the perspective as assessed in the supplied review, rather than independent examination of its cited experiments. The review notes that reference 112 concerns cochlear implants and is misplaced as visual evidence; the perspective’s explicit narrative and reference 38 still support its account of human shape perception. This citation problem limits reliance on that particular reference and does not establish that the reported human result is false.

The supplied review reports complete extraction of the perspective’s main text and references, with no indicated truncation or extraction problems. Its conclusions about shapes, coverage and safety were based on text and did not require inspection of figures. Nevertheless, this is a July 2025 account: the supplied record contains no subsequent search evidence establishing the field’s status through 1 November 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed functional demonstration: people with otherwise untreatable blindness independently use an implanted system for navigation, face recognition and ordinary reading across varied real-world settings. Evaluation should specify participant characteristics, task difficulty, assistance allowed and performance thresholds before testing. These are proposed criteria for making “useful, detailed sight” concrete, rather than published consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Independent navigation, face recognition and ordinary reading across real-world settings

completion_criteria.text: Proposed attribution and reproducibility requirements: controlled comparisons should establish how much performance depends on the device’s visual input, accounting for residual vision, memorized environments and nonvisual cues. Results should reproduce across participants, sessions and unfamiliar settings, with independent replication where feasible. Finite testing would establish demonstrated breadth across those conditions, not universal performance in every environment or for every form of blindness.
completion_criteria.label: Visual-input-dependent performance reproduces across participants, sessions and unfamiliar settings

completion_criteria.text: Proposed durability and safety requirements: follow-up over years should establish whether useful performance persists, how stimulation thresholds and calibration needs change, and whether neurological or tissue harms remain within prospectively defined acceptable limits. A convincing protocol would specify follow-up duration, adverse-event limits, device failures and maintenance requirements. Years of durability are an intended demonstration target, not a duration validated by the supplied source.
completion_criteria.label: Useful performance persists for years within predefined safety limits

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: report achieved visual detail, field coverage and everyday task performance alongside training burden, dependence on assistance and conditions in which the device fails. These measurements should make clear whether success represents a limited but useful visual aid or the broader detailed-sight capability proposed here. Participant selection should also make explicit the condition of the surviving visual pathways and cortex, without assuming that one successful group establishes suitability for all causes of blindness.
completion_criteria.label: Report visual capabilities, practical burdens and participant suitability limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison: NRL-16, “Biologically repair the injured visual pathway,” shares the goal of restoring vision but proposes biological repair, whereas NRL-08 supplies visual information through cortical stimulation. The approaches could be complementary. Only NRL-16’s title is supplied, so the record does not establish which injuries it addresses or whether it could repair extensive destruction of visual brain circuits.

Roster-based comparison: NRL-17, “A durable bidirectional neural interface for movement and sensation,” overlaps in long-term tissue compatibility, stimulation reliability and conveying sensory information to the nervous system. NRL-08 has the specific endpoint of useful cortical sight; NRL-17 has a broader movement-and-sensation interface goal. NRL-07, “A dependable neural communication channel for profound paralysis,” also concerns reliable neural interfaces, but its stated endpoint is communication rather than visual restoration.

Roster-based comparison: NRL-02, “A general predictive theory of neural circuit computation,” could inform how stimulation produces meaningful neural activity. NRL-03, “Whole-brain, cellular-resolution recording during natural behavior,” could provide research capabilities relevant to understanding circuit responses. Neither title establishes a prerequisite for cortical visual prostheses: practical encoding might advance without a general theory or whole-brain recording.

Roster-based comparison: NRL-06, “Replace lost brain tissue while preserving learned function,” addresses a different problem that may become relevant when necessary brain circuits have been destroyed. NRL-08 primarily seeks to use surviving circuits through an implanted interface. Replacing tissue and restoring cortical visual input remain distinct innovations, and the supplied roster does not establish that either would solve the other’s barriers.

change_log.reason: The supplied record does not establish subsequent developments through 1 November 2026.

change_log.reason: The review supports these specific experimental details and their different species and interface scopes.

change_log.change: Integrated the encoding, simultaneous resolution-and-coverage, stimulation-safety and chronic interface-stability barriers.
change_log.reason: These complementary scientific and engineering distinctions explain why shape perception does not establish useful, detailed sight.

change_log.change: Qualified recipient suitability and downstream benefits as mechanistic reasoning and conditional possibilities.
change_log.reason: The source does not establish clinical eligibility rules, outcomes by blindness etiology or the proposed everyday benefits.

change_log.reason: The final inputs include NRL-16’s title but no detailed scope or evidence supporting that stronger relationship.

change_log.reason: The citation defect limits one supporting reference without negating the perspective’s explicit narrative or its other cited support.

unresolved_issues: Developments after July 2025, including the field’s status through 1 November 2026, are not established by the supplied record.
The underlying human and monkey experiments were not independently assessed in the supplied review; their detailed protocols, participant scope and performance measures remain outside this record.
The relationship between blindness etiology, surviving visual circuitry and suitability for cortical prostheses remains unspecified.
Task thresholds, participant criteria, follow-up duration, acceptable adverse-event limits and practical maintenance requirements need a prospective evaluation protocol.
NRL-16’s detailed scope remains unavailable. The recommendation to remove the unsupported circuit-repair assertion was adopted; its roster title supports only a broad comparison.

brief.title: Useful, detailed sight through a brain implant
possible: Some people whose eyes or optic nerves can no longer carry visual information could navigate independently, recognize faces and read ordinary text. A camera would send information to an implant that stimulates the visual cortex, the brain region that processes sight.
why: Restoring access to visual information could give people greater independence in travel, communication, education and work. The implant would deliver information directly to the brain, bypassing the damaged pathway from the eyes.

sources.who: Robin Kim and colleagues at Rice University
sources.showed: Their perspective reviews how patterned brain stimulation can produce recognizable shapes. Their computer simulation found that independently controlled stimulation sites produced more varied brain activity.
sources.quote: Single-channel stimulation activates the entire cortical column, resulting in highly synchronized, low-dimensional neural activity.
sources.cited_for: The work explains why precise stimulation across space and time matters for artificial sight.
sources.not_established: The simulation and reviewed shape experiments do not establish detailed, practical sight.

sources.who: Michael P. Barry, Philip R. Troyk and collaborators
sources.showed: This preprint reports camera-guided visual benefits in a blind participant whose wireless implants remained functional for over three years. A heat-sensing camera reduced distracting visual information.
sources.quote:
Counterintuitively, pausing camera-based stimulation 
during more than half of each second improved performance.
sources.cited_for: Wireless implants can support camera-guided visual tasks and remain functional over years.
sources.not_established: The small feasibility study does not demonstrate detailed scenes, face recognition or ordinary reading across everyday settings.

sources.who: Fabrizio Grani, Eduardo Fernandez and collaborators
sources.showed: In two blind volunteers, recorded brain activity predicted whether stimulation produced perceived flashes of light, called phosphenes, and how bright they appeared.
sources.quote: our results indicate that subjective visual experience can be accurately predicted from the recorded neural activity.
sources.cited_for: Brain recordings could help relate stimulation settings to what a recipient perceives.
sources.not_established: Predicting isolated flashes does not establish automatic control of a stable, detailed visual scene.

sources.showed: A blind participant identified some letters and recognized object boundaries through stimulation from implanted electrodes, the small contacts that deliver electrical pulses.
sources.quote: Implantation and subsequent explantation of intracortical microelectrodes were carried out without complications.
sources.cited_for: Implanted contacts can produce distinguishable visual patterns in a blind person.
sources.not_established: Recognizing selected letters and boundaries does not establish ordinary reading or long-term safety.

sources.who: Michael S. Beauchamp, Daniel Yoshor and collaborators
sources.showed: Blind and sighted participants recognized letter shapes when electrical stimulation traced them across the brain’s visual map.
sources.quote:
In both sighted and blind participants, dynamic stimulation enabled accurate
recognition of letter shapes predicted by the brain’s spatial map of the visual world.
sources.cited_for: The order and timing of stimulation can turn separate flashes into recognizable forms.
sources.not_established: Recognizing traced forms does not establish a continuously updated view of everyday surroundings.

shown: Barry and collaborators report the closest step toward practical use: camera-guided visual tasks with wireless implants functioning for over three years in a blind participant. This preprint shows limited visual benefits, rather than complex scenes.

Beauchamp’s and Fernández’s teams have produced recognizable shapes or selected letters through brain stimulation. Grani’s team linked brain recordings to perceived flashes, offering a way to measure what stimulation produces.
missing: No system has demonstrated independent navigation, face recognition and ordinary reading together across varied everyday settings.
A reliable way to turn camera images into stable, detailed perceptions across a broad field of view remains missing.
Useful sight must persist as tissue responses and stimulation needs change, without unacceptable harm.

milestones.label: Independent navigation, face recognition and ordinary reading
milestones.explanation: People with otherwise untreatable blindness would have to perform these activities across varied real-world settings under predefined test conditions. This would establish practical, detailed sight.

milestones.label: Visual input drives repeatable performance across people and settings
milestones.explanation: Controlled tests would have to isolate the visual input’s contribution and reproduce benefits across people, sessions and unfamiliar settings. This would distinguish useful vision from memory or other cues.

milestones.label: Useful sight persists safely for years
milestones.explanation: Follow-up would have to show sustained performance within predefined safety limits while tracking changing stimulation needs, failures and maintenance. This would establish whether the benefit can last.

milestones.label: Visual abilities, daily burdens and suitability limits are clear
milestones.explanation: Studies would have to report visual detail, field coverage, task performance, training, assistance, failures and participant suitability. This would define the aid’s practical scope and who could benefit.

uncertain: Which causes of blindness leave enough working visual circuitry for the implant to help remains unclear.
The performance thresholds, follow-up length and acceptable harms needed to judge success remain unsettled.
It remains unclear how much training, recalibration and assistance everyday use would require.

page.title: Cortical prosthesis for reading, face recognition and navigation
page.definition: A camera and processor convert a scene into patterns of electrical pulses delivered by electrodes on or within the visual cortex, the part of the brain that processes vision. The pulses evoke visual sensations called phosphenes, often experienced as spots of light. The goal is for a person blinded by damage to the eyes or optic nerves to use those perceptions to read connected text, recognise people by their faces and navigate everyday environments.

goal.need: A 2018 industry-sponsored study estimated a potential US population of 82,000 for one implant’s proposed use in profound blindness from eye or optic-nerve damage. People with severe inherited retinal disease report difficulty reading and navigating even with phones, canes and sighted guides. Seeing print, faces and obstacles would give them information they value in daily life. When the optic nerve can no longer carry an image, a cortical implant offers another route, provided the visual cortex responds and the recipient learns to interpret the patterns.

figures.caption: Unaddressed distance vision impairment or blindness attributed to two causes.
figures.note: Estimates quoted in WHO’s fact sheet dated 10 February 2026. These include vision impairment and blindness; they do not estimate eligibility for cortical implantation.

statements.quote: to help people with ocular causes of blindness regain at least some functional vision.
statements.context: NEI describes the purpose of its supported research on the Orion cortical visual prosthesis.

statements.quote: The goal is useful visual perception: spots or patterns of light that may support orientation and visual tasks rather than recreate normal sight.
face recognition, outdoor navigation, reading, self-care
statements.context: NCT06117332 lists these as examples of everyday tasks for a Smart Bionic Eye. Its primary outcomes concern phosphene shape, pattern discrimination and scene understanding.

completion.title: Blind recipients read text, recognise faces and navigate using cortical prosthetic vision in daily life.
completion.criterion: The same blind recipients use an implanted, camera-driven cortical visual prosthesis to read continuous text, recognise faces and navigate in everyday environments. A registered clinical study establishes benefit attributable to visual input against device-off and appropriate control conditions, using its prespecified task, safety and follow-up criteria. This is an Atlas fallback: no common reading speed, face-recognition accuracy, navigation score or follow-up duration defines this combined capability.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback, drawing the task set from NCT06117332 and the natural-environment requirement from HOVER; no outside body located defines the combined completion test.
completion.basis: NCT06117332 names the three activities as intended uses. Its primary outcomes are phosphene shape, pattern discrimination accuracy and scene understanding performance. HOVER recommends controlled assessment of everyday activities, including speed and accuracy. The requirement to demonstrate all three abilities in the same recipients is an Atlas criterion. Published demonstrations include identification of selected letters and walking with phosphene cues in repeated navigation trials.

milestones.title: A cortical visual prosthesis obtains FDA authorisation for its first human investigation.
milestones.criterion: For a first-in-human US investigation requiring an investigational device exemption, the sponsor obtains FDA authorisation to begin the investigation of the specified cortical prosthesis. The application includes the investigational plan and a report of prior investigations.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, 21 CFR 812.20; this milestone concerns the US investigational-device pathway.
milestones.threshold_quote: A sponsor shall not begin an investigation for which FDA's approval of an application is required until FDA has approved the application.

milestones.title: A cortical visual prosthesis elicits light percepts with a measurable detection threshold in a blind person.
milestones.criterion: Vary stimulation amplitude and measure whether a blind recipient reports a phosphene. Estimate the amplitude associated with the protocol’s specified probability of detection. In the CORTIVIS psychometric test, that probability is 50%, and randomly interleaved trials without stimulation measure false reports.
milestones.set_by: CORTIVIS investigators, published stimulation protocol in Fernández et al. (2021). The quoted 50% definition was used for intracortical electrodes; measurable phosphene detection is also used with surface electrodes.

milestones.title: Blind recipients distinguish electrically evoked visual forms above the task’s chance level.
milestones.criterion: A blind recipient identifies which visual form a cortical stimulation pattern evokes in a forced-choice task. Accuracy exceeds the task’s chance level: one half for two equally likely alternatives or one third for three.
milestones.set_by: Visual psychophysics convention applied in Beauchamp et al. (2020) and Fernández et al. (2021): forced-choice discrimination exceeding chance. The quotation is from the intracortical study.
milestones.threshold_quote: The subject’s performance was always above chance level

milestones.title: Camera-driven cortical stimulation improves visually guided tasks relative to device-off performance.
milestones.criterion: A blind recipient performs the same visually guided task with camera-driven stimulation on and off. Performance with stimulation improves on the task’s specified measure under the study’s analysis. The ICVP analysis uses repeated measures within each participant and two-sided tests at a significance level of 0.05.
milestones.set_by: Device-on and device-off comparisons used by the Orion and ICVP investigators. The significance level is specific to the ICVP analysis.
milestones.threshold_quote: All visual function and functional vision assessments are performed both with the System ON and OFF.

milestones.title: A cortical implant evokes visual perception at a measurable threshold 72 months after implantation.
milestones.criterion: At 72 months after implantation, measure the stimulation threshold for eliciting a visual percept on individual electrodes or groups of electrodes. The Orion protocol specifies this assessment time for its surface array and gives no minimum fraction of electrodes that must evoke a percept.
milestones.set_by: Second Sight Medical Products, secondary visual-perception outcome and assessment schedule in the Orion early feasibility study, NCT03344848.
milestones.threshold_quote: 1 month, 6 months, 12 months, 24 months, 60 months, 72 months

milestones.title: A clinical study meets its endpoints for cortical-prosthesis reading, face recognition and navigation.
milestones.criterion: In controlled clinical testing, the same blind recipients use an implanted, camera-driven cortical prosthesis for continuous-text reading, face recognition and navigation. A registered study meets its prespecified efficacy endpoint for each activity and its prespecified safety endpoint.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback. No outside body identified defines a combined controlled clinical success criterion for these activities. NCT06117332 names the intended uses and registers other primary outcomes.

milestones.title: A cortical prosthesis prototype converts camera input into electrode pulses on the bench.
milestones.criterion: Test the camera, image processor, implant electronics and electrodes together on the bench. Camera images must drive the processor and produce the corresponding stimulation pulses at the electrode outputs.
milestones.set_by: Monash Vision Group, end-to-end bench demonstration under the Australian Research Council’s Special Research Initiative in Bionic Vision and Sciences.
milestones.threshold_quote: a complete system, from camera to electrodes

not_found: No public Orion pivotal-trial protocol defining numerical safety and efficacy success criteria was found.
No shared cortical-prosthesis threshold for reading speed, face-recognition accuracy, navigation performance or acceptable adverse-event frequency was found.
No published cortical-implant study was found demonstrating everyday continuous-text reading, face recognition and navigation in the same blind recipients.
No statement from a professional society or blindness organisation was found disputing the value or feasibility of this specific three-task goal.

results.finding: One blind participant had a phosphene-evoking baseline current of 4 mA at one surface electrode.
results.detail: A brief calibration identified currents required to evoke phosphenes at two electrodes; the paper also mapped their perceived locations.
results.quote:
First, a brief calibration procedure (see STAR Methods ) was
used to ﬁnd the current required to evoke phosphenes from
the two electrodes, resulting in baseline current values of 4 mA
for electrode F03 and 3.6 mA for electrode F01.

results.finding: One blind participant correctly identified 33 of 36 electrically evoked forms.
results.detail: The participant chose among three forms at 30 forms per minute; chance performance was 33%.
results.quote:
In a sequence of 36 trials, 33 forms were correctly
identiﬁed (92% correct versus chance rate of 33%, p = 10 /C012).

results.finding: Two blind ICVP recipients had measurable phosphene thresholds at approximately 63% detection probability.
results.detail: The investigators selected current adaptively and fitted Weibull curves to the yes/no responses.
results.quote:
Thresholds were defined as currents at which the
probability of detecting a phosphene was approximately 63%.

results.finding: Two blind ICVP recipients distinguished grating orientation above chance. Participant 1 reached 67% correct on the finest grating.
results.detail: Fine-grating discrimination in Participant 1 required head scanning, multiple phosphenes and pauses in stimulation.
results.quote:
Participant 1’s performance with stimulation decreased from 100% correct 
(95% CI: 72–100%) with 0.10 cpd to 67% correct (95% CI: 56–77%) with 2.4 cpd

results.finding: In one blind ICVP recipient, thermal camera-driven stimulation reduced occupied-chair localization error to 0.9°.
results.quote:
Participant 1’s MAE was 
reduced to 2.0–8.8° with the visible-light camera (P < 9×10–6, 
permutation test, 107 repetitions) and 0.9–4.3° with the thermal camera (P < 8×10–7, permutation 
test, 107 repetitions) (Figure 6b).

results.finding: Two blind ICVP recipients underwent repeated phosphene threshold testing, with follow-up extending to 43 months in one.
results.quote:
Long-term changes in stimulation current required to elicit phosphenes were detected for only 
7.2% of electrodes over Participant 1’s 43 months and none of Participant 2’s electrodes over 11 
months.

results.finding: One blind ICVP recipient successfully located and walked to an experimenter in 85% of thermal-camera trials.
results.detail: The task used three possible locations a few meters away and scored whether the participant came within arm’s reach.
results.quote:
17/20 trials (85%, 95% CI: 64–95%, P < 0.01, permutation 
test, 104 repetitions) with the thermal camera (Figure 6c).

results.finding: Intracortical stimulation in two blind volunteers yielded measurable current thresholds at 50% phosphene detection.
results.detail: The reported current summaries use a 170 μs reference pulse width. The authors pooled current-varied and pulse-width-varied experiments by expressing thresholds as charge per phase.
results.quote: The current amplitude at which the sigmoidal fit reached 50% was deemed the behavioral current threshold.

results.finding: Two blind volunteers reliably perceived phosphenes throughout six months of intracortical implantation.
results.detail: The paper pools threshold measurements across the implantation period without giving a separate threshold at the six-month visit.
results.quote: Furthermore, both participants were able to reliably perceive phosphenes induced by electrical stimulation throughout the entire implantation period.

results.finding: One blind Orion recipient reported a phosphene at a baseline current of 3.6 mA on electrode F01.
results.detail: Screening increased current on successive trials until a phosphene was reported. Session calibration also used reported visibility and brightness to set baseline currents.
results.quote:
First, a brief calibration procedure (see STAR Methods ) was
used to ﬁnd the current required to evoke phosphenes from
the two electrodes, resulting in baseline current values of 4 mA
for electrode F03 and 3.6 mA for electrode F01.

results.finding: One blind Orion recipient identified 92% of electrically evoked forms in a three-choice task.
results.detail: The three choices were C, U and backward C. In the two-choice task, the participant distinguished upward from downward lines.
results.quote:
In a sequence of 36 trials, 33 forms were correctly
identiﬁed (92% correct versus chance rate of 33%, p = 10 /C012).

Microstimulation mainly evoked elementary phosphenes at

results.finding: One ICVP recipient discriminated chair position with camera-driven stimulation (χ²=35). Off performance was at chance.
results.quote: Using a visible or thermal camera, the implantee successfully discriminated the direction of a walking person (χ�(2)=22.7) and the position of an unoccupied chair (χ�(2)=35). All test results without stimulation were at chance.

results.finding: Phosphene thresholds in one ICVP recipient remained mostly stable over 2.5 years.
results.quote: Thresholds may vary up to 240% across days (median 16%) but have mostly remained stable over 2.5 years.

results.finding: All 6 Orion recipients improved with the device on versus off on square and motion detection tests.
results.quote: After training and experience using the Orion system, all subjects demonstrated improvement with the system turned on versus off in visual function tests to detect a small square on a computer screen and detect movement across the visual field.

results.finding: In the 6-recipient Orion study, fewer than 4% of electrodes lost functionality.
results.detail: The release does not specify how many recipients underwent assessment at 72 months.
results.quote: All devices remained functional throughout the study with a loss of functionality on fewer than 4% of electrodes.

results.finding: In one blind participant, the camera-driven prototype used 16 implanted intracortical electrodes.
results.detail: The encoder converted camera images into electrode addresses and stimulation amplitudes for the CereStim 96.
results.quote:
These 16 electrodes were selected to stimulate via electrodes 
distributed over the entire UEA.

results.finding: One blind participant had a mean single-electrode phosphene threshold of 66.8 μA in the binary-search test.
results.detail: The single-electrode mean came from the binary-search procedure. The separate psychometric test used a Weibull fit to estimate the 50% detection threshold.
results.quote: The mean stimulation threshold for single electrodes was 66.8 ± 36.5 μA.

results.finding: One blind participant identified electrically evoked horizontal versus vertical lines with 81.4% accuracy.
results.quote:
The subject’s performance was always above chance level and 
across 22 sessions on 4 different days, the overall success rate was 
81.4%.

results.finding: One blind participant achieved 100% accuracy in four-position square localization with camera-driven stimulation.
results.quote:
The subject was able to correctly  
point to the white square 100% of the time (150 trials across 5 
days)

results.finding: One blind participant had measurable intracortical phosphene thresholds during a 6-month implant study.
results.quote: Although the duration of this study was limited to 6 months

results.finding: The award abstract describes the ICVP’s first human study as FDA-approved. Sample size is unstated.
results.detail: HHS TAGGS records the NIH award. The FDA approval statement appears in the project abstract, which supplies no FDA decision, IDE number or authorisation date.
results.quote: The proposed work to clinically test an intracortical visual prosthesis under an FDA-approved Early Feasibility Study

results.finding: In one blind ICVP recipient, camera-driven stimulation used electrode-group activation lists updated at approximately 20 Hz.
results.detail: The camera-driven trial recorded scalp EEG and phosphene persistence in the implanted participant.
results.quote: Lists of electrode groups to activate to convey the camera image were updated every 40–50 ms, yielding a frame rate of approximately 20 Hz.

results.finding: In the two-recipient ICVP study, phosphene detection thresholds were estimated at a 63% hit rate.
results.detail: The paper gives the range of currents tested and the fitted detection probability. It does not tabulate individual threshold currents.
results.quote: The 63% hit‐rate threshold was determined assuming a Weibull distribution.

results.finding: One blind ICVP recipient had repeated phosphene threshold measurements spanning up to 1022 days.
results.quote: Threshold levels for each of 2030 electrode/parameter combinations were measured up to 55 times across up to 1022 days.

results.finding: Five blind Orion recipients reported surface-evoked phosphenes, with 50–59 electrodes mapped per recipient.
results.detail: The 0–8 mA range describes the screening protocol. The mapping counts establish phosphene elicitation, while the measured screening thresholds remain unreported.
results.quote:
Out of
the 60 electrodes implanted, 50 e59 electrodes were mapped per
subject.

definition = "A camera and processor convert a scene into patterns of electrical pulses delivered by electrodes on or within the visual cortex, the part of the brain that processes vision. The pulses evoke visual sensations called phosphenes, often experienced as spots of light. The goal is for a person blinded by damage to the eyes or optic nerves to use those perceptions to read connected text, recognise people by their faces and navigate everyday environments.". Reason: The present tense makes the combined everyday capability sound established, although Orion’s reported tests measure more limited abilities.

goal.need = "A 2018 industry-sponsored study estimated a potential US population of 82,000 for one implant\u2019s proposed use in profound blindness from eye or optic-nerve damage. People with severe inherited retinal disease report difficulty reading and navigating even with phones, canes and sighted guides. Seeing print, faces and obstacles would give them information they value in daily life. When the optic nerve can no longer carry an image, a cortical implant offers another route, provided the visual cortex responds and the recipient learns to interpret the patterns.". Reason: The WHO figures include people with less severe impairment, and the current paragraph omits the activities that people with severe vision loss want to regain.

add statement by University of California, Santa Barbara, 2023 (updated 2026): "face recognition, outdoor navigation, reading, self-care". Reason: The sponsor’s list of intended uses identifies the connection to this goal and distinguishes those uses from its registered outcome measures.

edit completion: basis = "NCT06117332 names the three activities as intended uses. Its primary outcomes are phosphene shape, pattern discrimination accuracy and scene understanding performance. HOVER recommends controlled assessment of everyday activities, including speed and accuracy. The requirement to demonstrate all three abilities in the same recipients is an Atlas criterion. Published demonstrations include identification of selected letters and walking with phosphene cues in repeated navigation trials."; refs = [4, 5, 10, 21]. Reason: The basis should identify what the registered study actually measures and explain why the published navigation result falls short of the combined test.

add milestone after None: "A cortical prosthesis prototype converts camera input into electrode pulses on the bench.". Reason: The current sequence starts at regulatory authorisation and omits the demonstrated bench test of the complete camera-to-electrode system.

edit m1: criterion = "For a first-in-human US investigation requiring an investigational device exemption, the sponsor obtains FDA authorisation to begin the investigation of the specified cortical prosthesis. The application includes the investigational plan and a report of prior investigations.". Reason: The criterion mixes two sponsors’ investigation histories with the US authorisation requirement.

edit m2: criterion = "Vary stimulation amplitude and measure whether a blind recipient reports a phosphene. Estimate the amplitude associated with the protocol\u2019s specified probability of detection. In the CORTIVIS psychometric test, that probability is 50%, and randomly interleaved trials without stimulation measure false reports.". Reason: The criterion mixes participant and electrode counts with the detection test and leaves the meaning of its 50% threshold unclear.

edit m3: criterion = "A blind recipient identifies which visual form a cortical stimulation pattern evokes in a forced-choice task. Accuracy exceeds the task\u2019s chance level: one half for two equally likely alternatives or one third for three.". Reason: The applicable threshold is the chance rate for the choices offered, while the current criterion also contains individual participants’ scores.

edit m4: criterion = "A blind recipient performs the same visually guided task with camera-driven stimulation on and off. Performance with stimulation improves on the task\u2019s specified measure under the study\u2019s analysis. The ICVP analysis uses repeated measures within each participant and two-sided tests at a significance level of 0.05."; set_by = "Device-on and device-off comparisons used by the Orion and ICVP investigators. The significance level is specific to the ICVP analysis."; set_by_kind = "community_convention"; threshold_quote = "All visual function and functional vision assessments are performed both with the System ON and OFF."; threshold_ref = 9; refs = [9, 12, 5, 7]. Reason: The current threshold quote reports a participant’s result instead of specifying the comparison used to test for benefit.

edit m5: title = "A cortical implant evokes visual perception at a measurable threshold 72 months after implantation."; criterion = "At 72 months after implantation, measure the stimulation threshold for eliciting a visual percept on individual electrodes or groups of electrodes. The Orion protocol specifies this assessment time for its surface array and gives no minimum fraction of electrodes that must evoke a percept."; set_by = "Second Sight Medical Products, secondary visual-perception outcome and assessment schedule in the Orion early feasibility study, NCT03344848."; set_by_kind = "protocol"; threshold_quote = "1 month, 6 months, 12 months, 24 months, 60 months, 72 months"; threshold_ref = 13; refs = [13]. Reason: The registry specifies a 72-month perception-threshold measurement, which visit completion and electrical reliability alone cannot establish.

edit m6: criterion = "In controlled clinical testing, the same blind recipients use an implanted, camera-driven cortical prosthesis for continuous-text reading, face recognition and navigation. A registered study meets its prespecified efficacy endpoint for each activity and its prespecified safety endpoint."; set_by = "Atlas fallback. No outside body identified defines a combined controlled clinical success criterion for these activities. NCT06117332 names the intended uses and registers other primary outcomes.". Reason: The controlled clinical test is distinct from everyday use, but the criterion currently includes a search result and could be mistaken for an endpoint already registered by the Smart Bionic Eye study.
remove not found 1. Reason: The note about registry page rendering describes a retrieval issue rather than a gap in scientific or clinical evidence.

add not found: "No published cortical-implant study was found demonstrating everyday continuous-text reading, face recognition and navigation in the same blind recipients.". Reason: The absence of a published combined result is distinct from the existing note about the absence of a common numerical threshold.

add not found: "No statement from a professional society or blindness organisation was found disputing the value or feasibility of this specific three-task goal.". Reason: Doubts about restoring natural sight address a stronger claim than the three functional abilities in this entry.
remove statement 2. Reason: The Smart Bionic Eye statement gives only the registry update year and stops before the passage that identifies the relevant activities.
